topic: Thread Unjoinability: Automatic Program Termination via `std::terminate`
explanation: Assumption: If a function scope exits and an `std::thread` object goes out of scope, the thread resource is automatically cleaned up, similar to other RAII objects. Reality: An `std::thread` object must be explicitly joined (`t.join()`) or detached (`t.detach()`) before its destructor runs, provided it represents an actively executing thread (i.e., `t.joinable()` is true). If the destructor is called on a joinable thread, the program immediately calls `std::terminate`. Why It Fails: C++ mandates this behavior to prevent silent resource leakage (if it implicitly detached) or potential deadlock issues (if it implicitly joined). This rule means that raw `std::thread` objects require careful management, usually involving RAII wrappers (like a custom `ThreadGuard`) to guarantee joining or detaching even in the presence of exceptions.
practical_example: A complex function uses `std::thread` to launch background processing. An exception is thrown early in the function body. Stack unwinding occurs, the thread object destructor runs on a joinable thread, and the entire application immediately crashes instead of allowing the exception handler to take over.
